CausalChain: Chronic liver injury induces hypoxia → Hypoxia elevates HIF‐1α expression in HCC cells → HIF‐1α upregulates ENTPD2 expression → ENTPD2 converts extracellular ATP to immunosuppressive 5′‐AMP → Elevated 5′‐AMP promotes recruitment/accumulation of MDSCs in the tumor microenvironment → Accumulated MDSCs enhance immune checkpoint expression (e.g., PD‐1/PD‐L1) and suppress CTL activity → Dual targeting of ENTPD2 and PD‐1/PD‐L1 signaling can reverse immunosuppression.
Hypothesis: Dual inhibition of ENTPD2 and the PD‐1/PD‐L1 signaling axis will synergistically reduce MDSC‐mediated immunosuppression and restore effective CTL activity, thereby enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) emerges in the context of chronic liver inflammation, where hypoxia and immune suppression converge to hinder effective antitumor immunity. Recent studies have delineated a mechanistic link between hypoxia‐inducible factor‐1α (HIF‐1α)–mediated upregulation of enzymes such as ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase 2 (ENTPD2) and the accumulation of myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). ENTPD2 converts extracellular ATP to 5′‐AMP, promoting the local recruitment of MDSCs, which in turn enforce immune suppression through upregulation of checkpoint molecules such as PD‐1/PD‐L1. Here, we propose a novel combination therapeutic approach that simultaneously targets ENTPD2 and the PD‐1/PD‐L1 axis to disrupt this suppressive circuit. The dual inhibition strategy is expected to reduce MDSC accumulation, relieve T cell exhaustion and ultimately enhance cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) antitumor activity, potentially yielding improved clinical responses in HCC patients.
